articles.title: Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising mechanism that allows certain metals to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F), when similar materials typically become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, two experimental alloys reorganize their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible.
articles.content:
Scientists have uncovered an unexpected way certain metals can withstand extreme cold without becoming dangerously brittle. The discovery challenges long-standing ideas about how metals behave at extremely low temperatures and could help engineers develop tougher materials for some of the harshest environments imaginable.

The findings, published October 14 in Nature, reveal a previously unknown microscopic process that allows two experimental metal alloys to remain remarkably resistant to damage at just 20 kelvin, or -253°C (-424°F). The research was led by an international team from the University of California, Berkeley, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the University of Oxford.

Why Extreme Cold Makes Some Metals Brittle

Cooling a metal generally increases its strength, but this improvement can come with a serious drawback. Certain metals become increasingly brittle as temperatures fall, making them more likely to crack or break instead of bending under pressure.

This problem is particularly important for a family of materials known as body-centered cubic metals (such as iron, tungsten, and chromium). Their atoms are arranged in a specific crystal pattern that can make them especially vulnerable to brittle failure in extreme cold. At temperatures approaching absolute zero, a small crack that might ordinarily be accommodated by the metal changing shape can instead spread and cause a fracture.

However, researchers discovered that two experimental alloys made from niobium and titanium behave very differently. Even when cooled to -253°C, both materials maintained an impressive ability to withstand damage. Neither showed a measurable shift toward brittle behavior at the lowest temperature tested.

The explanation lies in a surprising change in how the metals respond to stress. Rather than relying on their usual method of deformation, the alloys activate a different microscopic process that helps prevent cracks from spreading.

A Hidden Mechanism Helps Metals Resist Cracking

Under normal conditions, body-centered cubic metals bend and change shape through the movement of tiny defects within their crystal structures. These defects, called dislocations, allow layers of atoms to shift relative to one another, helping the material absorb stress without breaking.

As temperatures drop, however, these dislocations become increasingly difficult to move. With fewer ways to accommodate the forces concentrated around a crack, the metal becomes more likely to fracture.

The newly studied alloys have another way to respond.

Researchers observed a process called nanoscale 'twinning', in which tiny sections of the metal's crystal structure rearrange into mirror-image patterns. This occurs alongside a localized change in the crystal structure itself.

When these newly formed regions encounter the boundaries separating neighboring crystals, they produce concentrated areas of stress. Those stress concentrations generate additional defects, giving the metal new opportunities to deform rather than crack.

The researchers compare this behavior to a road system finding alternative routes when its usual roads become blocked by ice. As extreme cold makes conventional deformation increasingly difficult, the newly formed crystal structures provide other pathways for the metal to accommodate stress.

By creating these new pathways, the material can continue absorbing forces around potential fractures instead of failing abruptly.

A Breakthrough for Metals Used in Extreme Environments

The findings suggest a new approach to developing structural metals that can withstand exceptionally low temperatures. Such materials could be valuable in energy systems, transportation, and aerospace engineering, where components may encounter severe thermal conditions.

Oxford corresponding author Professor Dong Liu (Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford) said: "For decades, the ductile-to-brittle transition has been viewed as a fundamental limitation of body-centered cubic metals. What surprised us is that these alloys remain remarkably damage tolerant even at 20 kelvin. By uncovering how twinning and phase transformation work together to generate plasticity before conventional dislocation motion, we identified a new pathway for designing structural body-centered cubic metals that can operate in extreme cryogenic environments. This class of materials will be extremely useful for components experiencing extreme hot and cold temperatures in one application."

The discovery also changes how scientists may need to think about what determines whether a metal becomes brittle. Previously, much of the emphasis was placed on how easily existing defects could travel through a material. The new results indicate that generating fresh defects may be just as important.

Lead author Dr. David Cook (University of California, Berkeley at the time of the study, now University of Cambridge) said: "Our results suggest we should change how we think about what governs the transition to brittleness for these metals. Traditionally, the focus was on how readily existing dislocations can move through a metal, but now it appears that the ability to create new dislocations at interfaces may also be critical. Using these insights, we may be able to design underlying microstructural conditions that allow a material to create its own routes to remain ductile at extreme temperatures."

How Scientists Tested Metals at -253°C

To investigate how the alloys performed under such punishing conditions, the team conducted experiments using the Engin-X instrument at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source in Oxfordshire.

The researchers used gaseous helium to cool metal samples to approximately -253°C. While directing a beam of neutrons through the materials, they used a specialized testing machine to stretch the samples by pulling from opposite ends.

This setup allowed the team to measure the forces the metals could withstand and determine how far they could stretch before breaking. The neutron measurements also helped researchers investigate what was happening inside the materials as they were deformed.

Afterward, the scientists examined the tested samples using powerful electron microscopes. These instruments revealed extremely small structural changes within the metal, including those near cracks that helped explain its unusual resistance to damage.

The team also used atom-probe analysis to determine how individual elements were distributed throughout the alloys. Combined with computer modeling, these measurements helped establish how the different microscopic processes worked together to prevent brittle failure.

The results offer more than an explanation for the surprising behavior of two experimental alloys. They identify a potentially useful strategy for designing metals that can remain tough even when conventional methods of deformation stop working, opening new possibilities for technologies that must operate in extreme cold.

The international collaboration included researchers from the University of California, Berkeley; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; the University of Oxford; the University of Bristol; the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source, Science and Technology Facilities Council; the University of California, Irvine; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory; Texas A&M University; and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery of metals that resist brittleness at extremely low temperatures, revealing a new microscopic mechanism. This breakthrough has broad implications for developing tougher materials for extreme environments, benefiting industries like aerospace, energy, and transportation. The story is focused, detailed, and describes a real-world impact with potential large-scale benefits.

articles.title: Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a bizarre bacterial defense system that works almost completely backward from anything seen before. Unlike typical bacterial immune systems that keep a deadly toxin under control until a virus attacks, this unusual mechanism waits until an infection begins before producing the DNA that switches on its lethal weapon. The infected bacterium then destroys itself, preventing the virus from multiplying and spreading to neighboring cells.
articles.content:
Scientists at Gladstone Institutes have discovered an unusual bacterial immune system that operates in almost the opposite way of previously known defenses. The surprising mechanism allows bacteria to activate a deadly self-destruct process when viruses attack, potentially offering new ideas for developing medical treatments and gene-editing technologies.

The findings, published in Molecular Cell, reveal how a group of bacterial defense systems called "type VI retrons" use an unexpectedly complex sequence of molecular events to fight infection. Unlike other retrons, these systems rely on DNA to activate a toxin rather than keep one suppressed.

Understanding this unusual process could do more than expand scientists' knowledge of bacterial immunity. It may also provide a foundation for designing more effective DNA-editing tools, potentially allowing researchers to correct harmful genetic mutations with greater precision.

"This is, by far, the strangest of the retron systems that we or anyone else has come across," says Gladstone Investigator Seth Shipman, PhD, senior author of the new study. "These retrons operate with Rube Goldberg-level complexity, using molecular mechanisms that we would never have thought to invent, but that we'll use in future technologies."

How Bacteria Sacrifice Themselves to Stop Viruses

Bacteria face constant threats from viruses known as phages, which infect bacterial cells and use their machinery to reproduce. Over time, bacteria have evolved a variety of defenses to prevent these viruses from spreading.

Among these defenses are retrons, molecular systems that can detect certain viral infections and trigger the infected bacterium to destroy itself. Although this sacrifice kills the individual cell, it prevents the virus from producing more copies and infecting nearby bacteria, helping protect the larger colony.

Retrons are also of considerable interest to scientists developing new genetic technologies. They can efficiently produce and deliver single-stranded DNA, making them promising tools for editing DNA inside human cells. Shipman's team and other researchers are investigating whether these capabilities could eventually be used to correct mutations responsible for disease with exceptional accuracy.

Until now, scientists believed they understood the basic way retron defenses operate.

In previously studied retrons, a toxic protein is already present inside an uninfected cell, but its harmful effects are held in check by short pieces of single-stranded DNA. When a phage infects the bacterium, it disrupts this protective arrangement, allowing the toxin to act. The resulting cell death prevents the virus from spreading.

The newly investigated type VI retrons, however, did not appear to follow this familiar pattern.

A Bacterial Immune System That Works Backward

Researchers first became suspicious that type VI retrons were different when they could not detect the single-stranded DNA normally associated with these systems.

"The way we typically detect retrons inside uninfected cells is by looking for this single-stranded DNA," says Karen Zhang, a PhD student in Shipman's lab and lead author of the study. "But type VI retrons caught our attention because they didn't appear to have this signature. It was very odd, and we wondered if they might be broken."

Despite their unusual behavior, experiments showed that bacteria carrying type VI retrons could still defend themselves against phage infections. The systems were clearly functional, even though they lacked the expected molecular signs of activity.

"That kicked off a long molecular odyssey," Shipman says. "Whenever we tried the experiments we normally use to study retrons, they would fail, so we kept having to think of new ways to figure out how these retrons work."

After extensive investigation, the team discovered that type VI retrons reverse a key step in the usual defense process.

Rather than maintaining a substantial supply of single-stranded DNA and toxin before infection, these retrons produce little detectable DNA and no noticeable amount of toxin in healthy cells. The arrival of a phage triggers a sharp increase in DNA production.

As the DNA accumulates, it interacts with an RNA molecule that has been preventing the toxin from being made. This interaction removes the restriction, allowing the bacterium to rapidly produce the toxic protein.

The toxin appears to be an exceptionally small protein that inserts itself into the bacterium's surrounding cell membrane. By disrupting the membrane's stability, it causes the infected cell to die, stopping the viral infection from spreading.

In other words, the DNA acts as an activation switch rather than a restraint. Instead of preventing an existing toxin from causing harm, it helps turn on toxin production only when the bacterium detects a threat.

"It's almost the mirror-image version of how we traditionally view retrons, because the DNA switches on toxin production instead of inhibiting an already-produced toxin," Zhang says. "It would be fascinating to explore how bacterial evolution could have resulted in such a complex molecular system -- whether type VI retrons are older or newer than other retrons, or whether they're a stepping stone between different types."

An Unusual Discovery Required New Experiments

Figuring out how type VI retrons function proved unusually difficult. Many established techniques that scientists use to examine retrons repeatedly produced no useful results, forcing the team to develop new experimental strategies and adapt existing methods.

One particularly important challenge involved detecting the DNA produced by type VI retrons in cells that had not been infected.

After conventional tests failed, the researchers tried a technique called Spacer-seq, which had previously been developed in Shipman's laboratory. The method uses components of CRISPR-Cas, another bacterial immune system, to record molecular activity inside cells.

CRISPR-Cas is best known for its role in modern gene-editing technologies, but bacteria originally evolved these systems as defenses against viruses. Spacer-seq takes advantage of this natural machinery to help researchers investigate what happens inside cells.

The alternative approach finally revealed a trace amount of single-stranded DNA that earlier experiments had missed.

"We had just about given up hope that any DNA was being made when this approach finally revealed a very, very low level of production in uninfected cells," Zhang says.

This breakthrough encouraged the researchers to continue investigating. Additional experiments confirmed that type VI retrons produce DNA at very low levels under normal conditions and substantially increase production only after a phage enters the cell.

The findings explained why the defense system had appeared inactive in earlier tests and revealed the unusual sequence of events responsible for its antiviral activity.

Could This Strange Bacterial Defense Lead to New Medical Treatments?

The discovery is already influencing research in Shipman's laboratory, where scientists are exploring ways to transform the type VI retron's natural machinery into useful technologies.

One promising application involves developing synthetic molecular sensors and switches that can regulate gene activity. Such systems could potentially allow researchers to control when particular genes are activated or suppressed, opening new possibilities for studying disease and designing treatments.

"This system represents a unique way to potentially build a molecular sensor and switch encoded in DNA and RNA, that no one has thought of before," Zhang says. "Synthetic sensors and switches have many possible applications, both in treating disease and in designing experiments to better understand how certain diseases operate."

Another possibility involves the retron's unusually small but powerful toxins. Because these proteins can disrupt bacterial membranes and kill cells, researchers are investigating whether they could be adapted into new antimicrobial treatments.

Such therapies could potentially target harmful bacteria responsible for human infections, providing a new approach to combating bacterial disease.

These medical applications remain under development, but the discovery offers researchers a molecular design that would have been difficult to imagine without studying nature's existing solutions.

"This study highlights why it's so important for a molecular technology development lab like ours to keep looking to nature for inspiration," Shipman says. "We can use what evolution has given us as starting points to build complex machines that would have been tremendously hard to even conceptualize."

The research also raises intriguing questions about bacterial evolution, including how such an elaborate defense arose and whether type VI retrons represent an earlier, later, or intermediate stage in the evolution of these immune systems.

For scientists seeking new ways to manipulate DNA, control genes, and fight infections, this backward-acting bacterial defense could provide an unexpected starting point.

The research, "Reverse transcribed ssDNA derepresses translation of a retron antiviral protein," was published in Molecular Cell on October 13, 2026.

Along with Shipman and Zhang, the authors include Matías Rojas-Montero, Darshini Poola, and Alejandro González-Delgado of Gladstone; Josepha Klas, Arturo Carabias, Dennis Zhang, Mario Mestre, Ruiliang Zhao, Ana Dávila-Hidalgo, Guillermo Montoya, and Rafael Pinilla-Redondo of the University of Copenhagen; and Lieza Chan and Kliment Verba of UC San Francisco.

The research received support from the National Science Foundation, the Robert J. Kleeberg Jr. and Helen C. Kleberg Foundation, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, the Lundbeck Foundation, the Fulbright U.S. Student Program, the Junta de Castilla y León and European Social Fund Plus, the European Molecular Biology Organization, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the European Research Council, and the Villum Foundation.

articles.title: Fish pay attention to one influential neighbour in virtual reality
articles.summary: Observing interactions between real and virtual rummy-nose tetra fish shows that, within a group, each individual takes cues from only one influential neighbour
articles.content:
Observing interactions between real and virtual rummy-nose tetra fish shows that, within a group, each individual takes cues from only one influential neighbour

Virtual reality, but for fish David Villa, ScienceImage, CBI, CNRS, Toulouse

A virtual reality tailored to fish reveals that each animal may be paying attention to only a single, most influential neighbour. This finding may shed light on how animals move as groups without becoming overwhelmed by all the activity and interactions around them.

Fish form schools, milling about seamlessly and acting as a collective. But how does a single fish know what to do? Guy Theraulaz at the University of Toulouse in France and his colleagues attempted to answer the question by using virtual reality (VR) to better study interactions between five rummy-nose tetra fish (Hemigrammus rhodostomus).

“A fish in a group can perceive, simultaneously, many, many individuals, but perception is not equivalent to influence,” he says. “Does a real fish use all this information at once, or does it just focus on a few neighbours?”

Advertisement

The researchers put a single tetra fish in a hemispherical bowl and tracked its swimming with a camera while projecting four virtual tetra fish onto the bowl’s interior in such a way that they appeared real to the tetra. The projections and the camera were connected into a feedback loop, allowing the virtual tetras to react and adjust to the real fish. Theraulaz says that he and his colleagues previously studied tetras in observational experiments and developed a mathematical model for how they might interact. The virtual reality setup allowed them to test that model.

Specifically, they tested three hypotheses: that a single fish would have the most influence on the real tetra’s behaviour; that two tetras would jointly be the most influential fish; and that the real tetra would pay attention to all four virtual fish. The team found clear evidence favouring the first case: as far as the real tetra was concerned, there was only one most influential fish at a time. This may be the case simply because it is easier on the fish, says Theraulaz. “By focusing on just one neighbour, the fish reduce their sensory and cognitive demand,” he says.

Iain Couzin at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior in Germany says that the new study confirms past ideas about tetra behaviour, which were largely pioneered by Theraulaz and his colleagues. It also underscores how powerful VR could be for eventually getting into the heads of animals as they make decisions, he says.

Studies of collective animal behaviour are difficult to perform because an individual animal in a group can’t be isolated without disturbing group behaviours that the researchers want to study, which makes it tricky to test specific hypotheses. But making some animals virtual and fully under researchers’ control sidesteps this problem. Overall, VR leads to endless opportunities for experimenting, says Guy Amichay at Northwestern University in Illinois.



“You could technically design any virtual world you want,” he says. Couzin says that it would be exciting to apply the new method to other species of fish for whom no mathematical models exist.

Therauluz and his colleagues now want to advance their experiment by making some of the virtual fish act stressed, as if they were facing a predator, and then see whether this would affect the real tetra through their interactions.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a novel scientific breakthrough using virtual reality to study animal behavior, specifically how fish interact within groups. This research has broad implications for understanding collective animal behavior and cognitive processes, with potential applications across species. The use of VR as a tool for animal behavior experiments represents an innovative technological advancement with meaningful scientific impact.
articles.personality_title: Virtual reality reveals how fish follow one key neighbour in groups
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Fish often swim in groups called schools, moving smoothly together. Scientists have wanted to understand how a single fish decides where to swim when surrounded by many others.

**What happened** – Researchers at the University of Toulouse created a special virtual reality (VR) setup for fish. They placed a real rummy-nose tetra fish in a bowl and showed it four virtual fish on the walls that moved like real ones. The virtual fish reacted to the real fish’s movements, allowing scientists to watch how the real fish responded.

**Impact** – The study found that each fish pays attention mostly to one important neighbour at a time, rather than all the fish around it. This helps the fish avoid confusion and makes it easier to decide where to swim. Using VR to study fish behavior is new and lets scientists control the environment in ways that were not possible before.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using virtual reality, scientists discovered that fish focus on following just one key neighbour to swim smoothly in groups.
articles.personality_title_fr: La réalité virtuelle montre que les poissons suivent un voisin clé dans le groupe
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les poissons nagent souvent en groupes appelés bancs, bougeant ensemble de façon fluide. Les scientifiques veulent comprendre comment un poisson décide où nager quand il est entouré de nombreux autres.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Toulouse ont créé une réalité virtuelle (VR) spéciale pour les poissons. Ils ont placé un vrai tétra à nez rouge dans un bol et lui ont montré quatre poissons virtuels sur les parois qui bougeaient comme de vrais poissons. articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los peces suelen nadar en grupos llamados cardúmenes, moviéndose juntos de manera fluida. Los científicos querían entender cómo un pez decide hacia dónde nadar cuando está rodeado de muchos otros.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Toulouse crearon una realidad virtual (VR) especial para peces. Colocaron un pez tetra de nariz roja real en un bol y le mostraron cuatro peces virtuales en las paredes que se movían como peces reales. Los peces virtuales reaccionaban a los movimientos del pez real, permitiendo a los científicos observar sus respuestas.

**Impacto** – El estudio encontró que cada pez presta atención principalmente a un vecino importante a la vez, no a todos los peces alrededor. Esto ayuda a evitar confusión y facilita la decisión de hacia dónde nadar. Usar VR para estudiar el comportamiento de los peces es algo nuevo que permite controlar el entorno de formas antes imposibles.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo planea hacer que algunos peces virtuales actúen asustados, como si hubiera un depredador cerca, para ver si el pez real reacciona diferente. Esto podría enseñar más sobre cómo los peces responden al peligro en grupo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Usando realidad virtual, los científicos descubrieron que los peces se enfocan en seguir a un vecino clave para nadar en grupo sin problemas.
